text: Chapter 6 is this course's capstone project: build, train, and honestly benchmark a small quantum classifier end to end. Every choice in this first lesson, dataset, feature count, label balance, determines whether the rest of the project is even feasible on the techniques this course actually covers.

Given everything from earlier chapters, barren plateaus getting worse with qubit count, parameter-shift cost scaling with parameter count, and classical simulation cost scaling exponentially, this project's dataset needs few features, roughly two to four, so angle encoding needs only that many qubits; a binary or small class count; and data that's real, publicly available, and already known to be at least partially separable by simple classical methods.

The working dataset for this project is the scikit-learn Iris dataset, reduced to two features, petal length and petal width, and two classes, Setosa versus not-Setosa. Under angle encoding, that needs exactly two qubits, comfortably simulable and far from barren-plateau territory. Iris is real: actual flowers, measured by Edgar Anderson in 1935, not a synthetic toy generator.

Using a classic, well-characterized benchmark dataset is the right choice here, not a cop-out, because it means the classical baseline comparison in a later lesson is measuring against something the field already understands well, meeting the fair-comparison standard from Chapter 1. A fabricated dataset tuned to flatter one method would make any comparison meaningless.
Next lesson assembles the actual two-qubit circuit for this project, encoding real Iris measurements and tracing one full forward pass and one gradient update by hand.
